::: {.project-lede}
When higher-level sample sizes are small, variance components can be weakly identified and prior choices can materially affect Bayesian multilevel estimates. This study introduces a transparent inverse-gamma construction that matches the prior mode to an interpretable variance target while keeping prior strength explicit.
:::

## Abstract {#abstract}

The paper proposes a mode-matched inverse-gamma strategy for variance components in Bayesian multilevel models. A substantively plausible or empirically grounded variance value is used as the target prior mode, while a separate shape parameter controls prior concentration. The method was evaluated in a Monte Carlo study and in a disjoint reference-sample illustration using TIMSS 2019 U.S. Grade 8 data. The broader goal is not to prescribe a universal prior, but to make prior location, prior strength, calibration source, and sensitivity explicit.

Crossing these factors produced **162 two-level random-intercept conditions**, with **200 replications per condition**. The study compared maximum likelihood, a Bayesian baseline prior, IG(0.01, 0.01), and mode-matched inverse-gamma priors. It included both an idealized true-mode benchmark and a disjoint reference-sample calibration illustration.

::: {.mini-grid}
<div><strong>32,400</strong><br><span>generated simulation datasets</span></div>
<div><strong>243 → 30 schools</strong><br><span>non-overlapping TIMSS reference and target samples</span></div>
<div><strong>Variance recovery</strong><br><span>bias, RMSE, interval coverage, and interval width</span></div>
<div><strong>Parameter sensitivity</strong><br><span>variance components versus fixed effects</span></div>
:::

## Key Findings {#key-findings}

- **Mode-matched priors improved variance-component estimation in the benchmark conditions.** Gains were most evident for between-level residual variance with small or moderate numbers of clusters, including lower RMSE and mean absolute relative bias than the Bayesian baseline and IG(0.01, 0.01) specifications.
- **Reference-informed calibration helped, but was not automatically optimal.** In the disjoint reference-sample illustration, the calibrated prior reduced RMSE and interval width relative to the baseline, while relative-bias performance was less favorable when the number of clusters was very small.
- **Fixed-effect point estimates were comparatively stable across Bayesian prior choices.** Prior sensitivity was concentrated more strongly in variance components than in fixed effects.
- **Calibration and sensitivity analysis are part of the method.** The results support documenting where prior information comes from, separating reference and target data when possible, and checking how conclusions change across plausible prior strengths.

## Contribution to my research program

This paper anchors my broader work on **Bayesian calibration under limited information**. Related projects extend prior calibration to multilevel item-response models, software translation, random-effect covariance structures, and applied guidance for selecting and reporting variance priors.
